body: **Decision:** Use Orama Zetta as both the control-plane state store (deployed graph, node registry, run history, secret-refs, audit) and the data/compute substrate. **Why:** one engine, no extra database to operate; self-hosting on the thing we deploy. **Supersedes** orama-platform-1's Postgres-spine decision. **Risk:** Orama Zetta lacks transactions + leader election today (see RSK control-plane-on-CRDT).
summary: Control-plane state lives in Orama Zetta's CRDT-replicated store; the control plane self-hosts on the engine it deploys.
title: Orama Zetta is the spine (no separate Postgres control plane)

body: **Decision:** The execution graph / IR is Orama Zetta-native with two forms: (1) **code** — embedded **Lua** (or **Orly**, our DSL) that calls into Orama Zetta's native C++ cluster API; (2) **data** — a **tabular Parquet/CSV/Automerge** representation of the graph/IR. The two are composable (call back and forth) OR usable independently (OR). **Why:** this is also the **primary extensibility mechanism** — e.g. enterprise-specific infrastructure-creation rules can be a set of Lua/Orly scripts and/or Parquet files (code AND data). No dependency on orama-platform-1. **Refines** ADR-2. **Implication:** the GUI inspects/edits both forms; the compiler can emit either.
summary: The IR has two interchangeable forms — code (Lua | Orly) and tabular data (Parquet/CSV/Automerge) — usable together or either alone; it is also the primary extensibility mechanism.
title: Dual-form, Orama Zetta-native execution-graph IR

body: **Decision:** Define **common interfaces** (Runner, Extension) with swappable **concrete implementations**. R1 runners: **Lua** and **Orly**; **Python** (and others) added later behind the same interface. An **Extension** is a unit of customer/enterprise extensibility = **code** (Lua/Orly) and/or **data** (Parquet/CSV/Automerge). **Why:** keeps the platform open and future-proof without re-architecting; the extension system is how enterprises inject their own infra rules and logic. **Relates to** ADR-10 (the IR forms) and ADR-16 (the interface-first principle).
summary: Everything is built behind common interfaces; concrete runners = Lua + Orly now, Python later. Extensions = code and/or data.
title: Runner & Extension abstraction via common interfaces

body: **Decision:** All runner/extension code (Lua/Orly now, Python later) executes in a **capability-scoped, deny-by-default sandbox**. It can only touch the Orama Zetta API/data explicitly granted via **capability tokens scoped to the invoking user's key/access**; **no filesystem or network egress by default**; **every API call is audited**. **Approval gates apply to shared / enterprise-published extensions**, not every personal run. **Why:** arbitrary code runs next to customer data — this is load-bearing for the 'no egress / governed' promise. **Relates to** ADR-6 (key-scoped governance), NFR-1 (no egress), FEAT-9 (governed self-service); **mitigates** the arbitrary-code risk (RSK-7).
summary: Extension code gets no ambient authority; capability tokens scoped to the invoking user's key; no fs/network egress by default; all API calls audited; approval gates for shared/enterprise-published extensions.
title: Capability-scoped, deny-by-default extension sandbox

body: **Decision:** Provide **Orly**, a first-party DSL, as a **Lua alternative** for the code form of the IR and for extensions. Orly is a concrete **Runner** behind the common interface (ADR-11), capability-sandboxed like Lua (ADR-12). **Why:** a higher-level, inspectable, safer-by-construction plan language tailored to Orama Zetta orchestration; users can choose Lua (general) or Orly (our DSL). Draws on the orly concept from orama-platform-1 but is implemented Orama Zetta-native, not inherited.
summary: Orama ships its own DSL, Orly, as an alternative to Lua for the code-form IR/extensions.
title: Orly — first-party DSL (Lua-alternative runner)

body: **Decision:** The Orama Zetta desktop GUI is built on Orama Zetta's existing **native SDL3 + Dear ImGui headed mode** — **not** a Tauri/web shell. The desktop **is a cluster node** (zero IPC, native C++). **Migration** from the existing Amaro Tauri desktop consists of **reading/importing the data from that app's SQLite database** into Orama Zetta (see TR-1). **Why:** one native binary, desktop-is-a-node, fast for dense graph/data views; consistent with 'R1 on what exists.' **Relates to** FEAT-10 (GUI surface), TR-1.
summary: The GUI is Orama Zetta's native SDL3/Dear ImGui headed mode (no Tauri/web); the desktop is itself a cluster node; migration from the Amaro Tauri app = import its SQLite DB.
title: Native SDL3/ImGui desktop = cluster node; migrate via SQLite import

body: **Decision:** The installer/GUI/desktop **node application is a coordinator/orchestrator** — **infrastructure orchestration IS the platform-engineering job.** It talks to cloud/infra APIs through a **Cloud Interface** abstraction with swappable concrete implementations: (a) **local CLI** wrappers (`aws`, `az`, `gcloud`, `kubectl`, …) and (b) **direct HTTP endpoint** calls (no local CLI required) — both valid. As part of orchestration it can **deploy additional headless Zetta nodes** into the target infrastructure. Because the local desktop is **just another cluster node**, a properly authenticated user can **fire up a different desktop and orchestrate from that node** too. **Refines** ADR-7 (placement dial). **Relates to** FEAT-4 (deploy), IR-1 (infra integration), ADR-16.
summary: The desktop/node app is a coordinator/orchestrator; it talks to cloud APIs through a Cloud Interface (concrete impls: local CLI e.g. aws/az/gcloud/kubectl, OR direct HTTP); it deploys headless Zetta nodes into target infra; any authenticated node can orchestrate.
title: Zetta orchestrates infrastructure via a Cloud Interface abstraction

body: **Decision:** Build everything by **declaring common interfaces**, with each concrete implementation implementing those interfaces. Applies across the platform: **Runner** (Lua/Orly/Python), **Extension** (code/data), **Cloud Interface** (CLI/HTTP), storage tiers, and future runners/providers. **Why:** this is the platform's extensibility and future-proofing spine — add a runner, a cloud provider, or a storage backend without re-architecting. **Generalizes** ADR-10/11/12/15.
summary: The platform's extensibility spine: common interfaces (Runner, Extension, Cloud Interface, storage tier, …) with swappable concrete implementations, declared up front.
title: Interface-first / pluggable-implementations architecture

body: **Decision:** Any compute-heavy algorithm — model **training**, **inference**, **DDF (distributed dataframe) operations**, **data engineering**, **inference serving** — is **re-implemented natively in C++ and/or CUDA (or other kernel languages)** and runs as a **cluster-parallel / cluster-concurrent** operation across Orama Zetta nodes. **Why:** (1) native reimplementation is now cheap/fast with Claude Code; (2) because we **control the infrastructure** (and its cost), we can parallelize or run concurrently at the **appropriate cluster level** — the source of the cost/performance advantage and the 'learns from your data, at scale' story. **Supersedes** the 'bridge via external pipeline / Python-runner training' options. **Relates to** ADR-4 (compute-near-data), ADR-16 (native impls behind common interfaces), FEAT-6 (learns from your data), FEAT-8 (compute-near-data). The R1 churn model may still bridge via the existing pipeline while native primitives are built (see roadmap).
summary: Re-implement training, inference, DDF ops, data engineering, and inference serving natively in C++/CUDA/kernel languages and execute them cluster-parallel/concurrent — not by wrapping external (e.g. Python) libraries.
title: Native (C++/CUDA) cluster-parallel compute for all heavy operations

body: **Decision (target):** each Orama Zetta node has a **cryptographic per-node identity**; nodes **mutually authenticate via mTLS** (wire the TLS that Corosio already supports — replacing today's plaintext TCP); **joining the cluster requires an enrollment token**; the right to **act as orchestrator** is **capability-scoped to the authenticated principal** (same capability model as the extension sandbox, ADR-12). **R1 reality:** runs **single-tenant inside the customer's network boundary** while mTLS/identity is being wired — documented as a hardening item, not pretended-done. **Mitigates** node impersonation (THR-2) and unauthorized orchestration (THR-4). **Relates to** ADR-15 (orchestration), ADR-12 (capabilities), FEAT-9.
summary: Every node has a crypto identity; nodes mutually authenticate (mTLS); cluster join needs an enrollment token; orchestration rights are capability-scoped to the authenticated principal. R1 runs single-tenant inside the customer boundary while this is wired.
title: Cluster trust model: mTLS + per-node identity + capability-scoped orchestration

body:
**Decision:** Node bootstrapping is **Orama Zetta-native.** The desktop is already a node; additional **headless Orama Zetta nodes** are stood up and **join the cluster via an enrollment token + mTLS** (ADR-18). The **Cloud Interface** (ADR-15) provisions/identifies the *target infrastructure* (CLI or HTTP concrete impls); Orama Zetta then drops its own nodes onto it.

**On k0s:** k0s / k0sctl / k0smotron is a **hint** for the *low-friction bootstrap UX* we want to match — a declarative host inventory → a single orchestrate action; token-based join; the clean split between a CLI surface (k0sctl/k0s over SSH) and an API surface (k0smotron CRDs over the k8s API). **We are NOT using k0s directly right now, and will NOT copy its API verbatim.** We may revisit k0s later as one concrete Cloud Interface target. The design stays centered on Orama Zetta and our own bootstrap primitives — k0s is reference inspiration only. **Refines** ADR-15; relates to ADR-18.
summary: Orama Zetta bootstraps and joins its own nodes (enrollment token + mTLS); the Cloud Interface provisions target infra. k0s/k0sctl/k0smotron is a low-friction-UX hint only — not used directly now, not an API to copy verbatim; maybe revisited later.
title: Node bootstrapping is Orama Zetta-native; k0s is inspiration only

body: **Decision:** A professionally-architected, versioned execution-graph IR is the artifact the GUI shows, validates, and deploys. **Open:** reuse 'orly' (orama-platform-1) vs. a Orama Zetta-native IR. **Why:** an inspectable graph (not a black box) is what makes generated systems reviewable and correct-by-construction.
summary: Compile intent/artifacts into an inspectable execution graph (connect→clean→model→index→serve→act).
title: Execution-graph IR as the compile target

body:
**Decision:** the Cloud Interface (ADR-15) supports **two provisioning modes**:

1. **Persistent cluster nodes** — long-lived Orama Zetta nodes that join via enrollment token + mTLS (ADR-18).
2. **Ephemeral burst / parallel-batch compute** — for **temporary workloads** (model **training**, large **DDF**/data-engineering jobs), the orchestrator **provisions N nodes at once**, runs the job **cluster-parallel** (ADR-17), then **tears them down**. Uses a parallel/batch infrastructure API where available.

**Identity at scale (design note, per ADR-18):** each burst node **probably still gets its own (short-lived) identity** — i.e. **bulk/batch enrollment** of per-node identities + capability tokens, revoked on teardown. *Open question:* the most efficient way to mint + revoke 20+ identities at once (batch enrollment vs. a group identity with per-node attestation). Tracked in RSK-9.

**Reference patterns (NOT chosen deps, NOT copied verbatim — same stance as k0s):** Azure **Batch** (`az batch pool create --target-dedicated-nodes N` + low-priority nodes → `job` → parallel `task`s), **VMSS** (`az vmss create --instance-count N`, Flexible orchestration), and **Spot/low-priority** capacity (`--priority Spot --eviction-policy --max-price`) for cost on interruption-tolerant training; equivalents on AWS (Batch) / GCP (Batch). We borrow the *shape* (burst-many, run, tear down, spot-for-cost), not the API. **Refines** ADR-15; relates to ADR-17, ADR-18, FEAT-6.
summary: Beyond long-lived cluster nodes, the Cloud Interface bursts N ephemeral nodes at once for temporary workloads (training, large DDF/data-eng jobs), runs cluster-parallel, then tears down. Each burst node still gets its own (short-lived) identity. Azure Batch/VMSS/Spot are reference only.
title: Two provisioning modes: persistent cluster nodes + ephemeral burst (parallel/batch) compute

## Context
The product/engine was previously called "ZettaDB". Leadership (Casey/Issac/Steve, 2026-06-24) confirmed the product is **Orama Zetta** — `oramasearch/zetta` *is* the product, not a separate engine wrapped by a product.

## Decision
Use **Orama Zetta** as the product name everywhere. Retire "ZettaDB". This is a **rename only — no functional or architectural change**. "Orama Zetta" is the current **working** name and may change.

## Consequences
- All artifacts, docs, and issues referencing "ZettaDB" are renamed to "Orama Zetta".
- `zetta` remains the repo/binary codename.
- Architecture and semantics are unchanged.
summary: The product is Orama Zetta (working name); the older name 'ZettaDB' is retired — a rename only, no functional change.

## Context
People don't care that Orama Zetta is a database — they care what it does for them. The kitchen/meals metaphor (2026-06-24): the engine is the kitchen; the **use cases are the consumable meals** — the emphasis is on the meals.

## Decision
All product framing **leads with the outcome** — "turns a question into running, deployed intelligence" (see the one-pager) — and demotes the technical substrate to "under the hood". Never lead with "a database".

## Consequences
- Vision/positioning artifacts, READMEs, repo descriptions, and the docs site lead value-first.
- Canonical framing: docs/projects/orama-platform-2/one-pager.md.
summary: Public framing leads with what Orama Zetta does for the user (intent -> deployed, correct intelligence), not the database category.
title: Lead with value, not "a database"

## Context
Kitchen/meals (2026-06-24): the meals (use cases) are what's consumable, not the kitchen (engine). "Go fat on use cases; ship a menu."

## Decision
Develop **use-case-first**. Each release must be a **consumable product** — a working slice of a use case (e.g. a customer gets a working production churn model within ~an hour). Backlog **priorities are set by a use case's dependency closure**, not by abstract release order. **UC-1 (Motive churn) is the first use case.**

## Consequences
- Prioritization traces UC-1's dependency graph (FEAT-1/2/3/4/6 + their deps).
- New use cases are added to the catalog; rinse and repeat.
summary: Releases are consumable use-case slices; priorities trace from a use case's dependency closure. Churn (UC-1) is the first use case.
title: Use-case-driven development; each release is a consumable product

## Context
The blueprint projects to ~278 GitHub issues; most are reference/design artifacts, not actionable work.

## Decision
Treat every tracking issue as a **request to produce an artifact** — software (a PR), docs (a PR), or a report (e.g. a test report). If no artifact is foreseeable, **close it with a reason (kept + linked, never deleted)**. Keep buildable work + risks + releases open. Driven by the `prune-backlog` skill.

## Consequences
- ~195 reference issues close (traceable, reopen-able); ~83 stay open.
- Closed != deleted; the blueprint stays intact.
summary: An issue = a request to produce software / docs / a report; if it produces none, close it (kept + linked, never deleted).
title: Backlog grooming: a tracking issue is a request to produce an artifact

body:
## Context
Most AI/data projects fail — they start backward (tech or data first, no defined problem), bolt stochastic models onto messy foundations, overpromise, and never reach production (Andrew Ng).

## Decision
The **central item is the AI/data project** (ENT-1 `Project`) — the unit a user creates, manages, and ships. Orama Zetta's real job is **data-project management**: the discipline that makes a project *succeed* — problem → right data → correct-by-construction model → governed deploy → monitor + iterate. A project is **user-managed** and composed of **optional components** the user controls.

## Consequences
- Vision, use cases, and UX are organized around creating + managing AI projects to success — not one-shot answers.
- The correctness gate (ADR-3 / FEAT-3), the lifecycle, and governance are the *management* discipline.
- Each use case (e.g. churn) instantiates as a Project.
summary: The central artifact is the AI/data project; Orama Zetta's job is managing AI projects to success (most AI projects fail).
title: AI projects are the central item; data-project management is the job

body:
## Context
Balance real AI intelligence (a model *trained on the data*) with being generic + reusable across teams. We are not a single-method tool.

## Decision
A **use case is a generic AI-project type** — the same template instantiates on any team's data (not a bespoke per-customer build). The **engine is general AI**: it featurizes + trains + serves **any** model type — XGBoost, RL, LLM fine-tuning — not one method. **Churn via featurize → XGBoost → SHAP is the first use case**; its optional components (recommended-action layer, LLM playbook) are user-managed. Keep use cases **simple, generic, reusable** — even a basic model is useful to most orgs.

## Consequences
- Build use cases as generic project templates with optional components, not bespoke pipelines.
- The catalog of use cases grows; the engine carries forward to the next one.
summary: A use case (e.g. churn) is a generic AI-project type any team runs on its own data; the engine trains/serves any model type, not one method.
title: Use cases are generic AI-project types; the engine is general AI

body: Refines ADR-17. Every compute-heavy operation (DDF ops, GBDT histograms/splits/predict, TreeSHAP, scoring) is expressed against a single `ComputeDevice` interface that exposes operators at the largest grain that still lets the cluster coordinator distribute the work. `CpuDevice` is the always-built reference backend; `CudaDevice` is an optional build. Adding hardware (Metal/ROCm/...) means implementing one new backend — zero algorithm or consumer changes. Operator-level (not primitive-kernel) per the decision this cycle. Relates to ADR-16 (interface-first) and ADR-17 (native C++/CUDA cluster-parallel compute).
summary: All heavy compute runs through a ComputeDevice operator interface; CPU and CUDA are pluggable backends; new hardware = a new backend, with no changes to any consuming code.
title: Operator-level accelerator interface (ComputeDevice; CPU+CUDA, pluggable backends)

body: Adds a typed message/event/task ('signal') layer over the existing equal-peer cluster transport, alongside SYNC/STATUS/LOREQ/LORES. It carries collectives (allreduce/broadcast/barrier/gather), work-stealing steal-requests, and ComputeJob dispatch. Compute partials (gradient histograms, partial aggregates) are transient signals — NOT durable CRDT state — so the Automerge document stays small and convergent. Reuses the replication/cluster capacity we already have. Relates to ADR-17, GLO-12.
summary: Distributed compute communicates via an ephemeral signal plane (RPC/event/task) layered on the existing cluster transport; compute partials never enter the replicated document.
title: Compute signal plane: RPC/event/task over the cluster (ephemeral, not CRDT)

body: Because the platform controls the infrastructure, a running job can scale while it runs: the autoscaler observes progress against a per-job objective (minimize cost, hit a runtime/latency target, adapt to data shape) and adds or removes nodes through the Provisioner. Work-stealing makes elastic membership natural — a new node steals work; a departed node's tasks are re-stolen. When hardware is GIVEN (not provisionable) the same model degrades to best-effort maximum utilization of the nodes present. Refines ADR-20; relates to FEAT-6, ARC-8.
summary: A ComputeJob is elastic: nodes are added/removed mid-flight and an autoscaler optimizes provisioning against a per-job reward (cost/runtime/latency/data-shape).
title: Elastic, reward-driven autoscaling of ComputeJobs

body: **Decision:** No graph deploys until it passes a correctness gate. **Why:** self-service that ships confidently-wrong pipelines is worse than the bottleneck it replaces; correctness is the differentiation vs. n8n/Zapier. R1 = compile/type/smoke checks; leakage + point-in-time planned and shown as not-yet-enforced.
summary: Validate (schema/leakage/point-in-time + correctness eval) before a graph can deploy.
title: Correctness gate before deploy

body:
## Context
Distribution today is replicate-to-all only (`ReplicationPolicy::ReplicateToAllNodes`, with a documented seam for sharded/quorum). To run on datasets larger than one node and to exploit burst capacity, data must be partitioned across nodes with compute running where the data lives.

## Decision
Replication strategy is a **per-table / per-database** property:
- **ReplicateToAll** (default, current behavior)
- **Partitioned** — each node holds a subset (shard) of the rows
- **PartitionedWithReplicas(rf)** — partitioned with a replication factor for fault tolerance

The **partition placement catalog is itself ReplicateToAll**, so every node has a global view of which partition lives where. **Compute-near-data**: DDF / SPMD ops execute against the partitions a node holds locally, rather than pulling all data per op.

## Consequences
- Extends the `ReplicationPolicy` seam with strategy + placement.
- Requires the `Partitioner` seam (ADR for it) and a placement/rebalance pass on membership change.
- Enables horizontal scale and elastic burst (provision nodes → partitions rebalance onto them).

Realizes FEAT-7 / FEAT-8; relates ADR-17 (native compute) and ARC-12 (DDF engine).
summary: Tables/databases choose replicate-to-all (default), partitioned, or partitioned-with-replicas; the partition catalog is replicated to all; distributed ops run on each node's local partition.
title: Per-table/database replication strategy + replicated partition catalog + compute-near-data

body:
## Context
A `partitioned` table needs two assignments: which **partition** a record belongs to, and which **node(s)** own a partition. These should be pluggable so placement can evolve (including ML-driven placement).

## Decision
Introduce a **`Partitioner`** seam with two responsibilities:
1. **record → partition** (e.g. hash of a key column, round-robin/surrogate for even balance)
2. **partition → node(s)** (e.g. rendezvous / consistent hashing so a join/leave moves only ~1/N partitions)

Use a **fixed partition count P (P >> nodes)** so rebalancing moves whole partitions (as blobs) rather than rehashing all rows. Ship basic partitioners first (Hash, RoundRobin + Rendezvous placement). **Later: models as partitioners** (the partitioner's job — assign record→partition, partition→node — can be performed by a learned model).

## Consequences
- New interface + a couple of concrete implementations.
- Placement recorded in the replicated partition catalog (system.dataset_partitions).

Relates ADR-16 (interface-first); supports the replication-strategy ADR.
summary: A Partitioner assigns each record to a partition and each partition to node(s); start with hash/round-robin + rendezvous placement; model-driven partitioners later.
title: Pluggable Partitioner seam (record to partition, partition to node)

body:
## Context
#408 deliberately left the Arrow/parquet-cpp dependency decision unmade. ADR-17 forbids foreign runtimes and keeps the engine dependency-light; the repo's ethos is from-scratch native code (e.g. a hand-written Automerge).

## Decision
**Hand-roll a read-only native Parquet reader** covering what the target datasets use: the row-group / column-chunk structure, plain + dictionary/RLE encodings, and snappy/zstd page decompression. Decode column chunks **straight into typed DDF columns (`DeviceBuffer`s)** — skip any JSON-row intermediate. No Arrow / parquet-cpp dependency.

## Consequences
- Bounded but real implementation effort; edge-case coverage risk tracked by the hand-rolled-parquet RSK.
- Revisit vendoring Arrow only if format coverage requirements outgrow the minimal reader.

Refines ADR-17; realizes the parquet half of #408.
summary: Hand-roll a read-only Parquet reader covering the encodings the datasets use, decoding column chunks directly into DDF DeviceBuffers; no Arrow/parquet-cpp dependency.
title: Native minimal Parquet reader (no Arrow/foreign dependency)

body:
## Context
SQL is one frontend. The product wants multiple frontends — SQL, a **simulated-Python** surface (the ideal; mirrors `load_dataset(...)` / dataframe idioms), optionally Lua/Orly — over the same functionality. The ExecutionGraph IR (ENT-3) already exists as the architect's compile target (ADR-2 / ADR-10, ARC-5).

## Decision
The **ExecutionGraph IR is the single lowering target (the 'core API')**. Frontends are thin parsers that emit IR; **none is privileged**:
- **SQL** dialect (exists) — e.g. `CREATE TABLE ... WITH (replication=partitioned, partitioner=hash)` + `COPY ... FROM '...' FORMAT parquet`.
- **Simulated-Python** (ideal) — assignments / calls / attribute-method chaining, plus **simulated libraries** (e.g. a `datasets.load_dataset(...)` shim) that emit IR ingest/compute steps.
- **Lua / Orly** (optional; ADR-13).

The data-loader, partitioning, featurize, train, and explain all become **IR step nodes**, so every frontend reuses the correctness gate (FEAT-3) and the distributed, compute-near-data executor (FEAT-5).

## Consequences
- New IR step-kinds/attributes for load + partitioning.
- Frontends are independent and additive.

Relates ADR-2, ADR-10, ADR-13, ARC-5; realizes FEAT-2 surface generalization.
summary: No frontend is privileged; SQL, a simulated-Python surface (incl. simulated libraries like HuggingFace datasets), and Lua all parse into the ExecutionGraph IR, which is gated and executed distributedly.
title: Multi-frontend core: SQL / simulated-Python / Lua lower to the ExecutionGraph IR

body:
## Context
The ExecutionGraph IR has an `index` step kind (connect→clean→model→index→serve→act) but no index engine exists. `oramacore-cpp` is a native C++ fulltext engine (benchmarked vs the Rust OramaCore) already vendored as a zetta submodule at `modules/oramacore-cpp`.

## Decision
Introduce a pluggable **IndexBackend** seam (build + query) behind an **Index** entity. The **native oramacore-cpp fulltext engine is the first backend**, backing `StepKind::Index`. This is the **first of many index types** (vector/semantic and others to follow). Indexes build compute-near-data over the table's partitions ([[Partition]]).

## Consequences
- New entities [[Index]] + [[IndexBackend]]; CMake wiring to the `modules/oramacore-cpp` submodule (PR opened separately).
- The index step in the IR resolves to an IndexBackend; future backends are additive (interface-first).

Relates ADR-16 (interface-first), ADR-17 (native, no foreign runtime).
summary: Indexes are built via a pluggable IndexBackend seam backing the IR index step (StepKind::Index); the native oramacore-cpp fulltext engine is the first backend. First of many index types (vector/semantic later).
title: Pluggable Index engine seam; oramacore-cpp native fulltext as the first index backend

body: **Decision:** Execute generated/user code on the Orama Zetta node holding the data via embedded Lua / a DataFrame API, sandboxed to the node's access scope. **Why:** no warehouse round-trip, no exfiltration — the data-locality moat. **Status:** Orama Zetta engine work, planned.
summary: Run user/agent code on the node where the data lives.
title: Compute-near-data via embedded Lua / DDF API

body: **Decision:** Pull source data (Snowflake first) into in-memory indexes, age to cold storage, re-warm on demand; serve from the local materialized copy. **Why:** the cost + locality story — stop paying warehouse prices for repeated queries. **Status:** Orama Zetta engine work, planned (largest engine bet).

body:
The end-to-end data plane for large external datasets.

**Pipeline**
1. **Ingest** — native parquet reader decodes column chunks → DDF columns; the parquet file is stored as a large-object **blob** (existing `LargeObjectStore` → CRDT `lo:` metadata → `ReplicatedBlobStore` gossip).
2. **Place** — a [[Partitioner]] assigns rows→[[Partition]]s and partitions→nodes per the table's [[ReplicationStrategy]]; placement recorded in [[system.dataset_partitions]] (ReplicateToAll).
3. **Compute-near-data** — DDF distributed ops (featurize/join/group-by/sort, GBDT, TreeSHAP) run on each node's local partition.
4. **Rebalance** — on membership change (Azure burst join/leave) partitions move (as blobs) to their new owners.

Builds on ARC-12 (DDF engine) and ARC-13 (Provisioner). Realizes FEAT-7 / FEAT-8.

body:
**Rule.** When the product exposes state for inspection or observability, the
**default** representation is a virtual, read-only table in the reserved `system`
database (à la `pg_catalog`): `system.zetta_*`. Examples already following this:
`system.zetta_nodes` (cluster + replication status), `system.zetta_deployments`,
`system.zetta_models`, `system.zetta_jobs`. New observable state — notably
**cloud / provider state** for the Cloud Inspector (providers, connection status,
provisioned bursts) — belongs here too (`system.zetta_cloud*`).

**How.** A `system` table is **computed at query time from the live in-memory
source** (`Node::…()` / a catalog), never a stored or hand-synced second copy.
Reach for a bespoke GUI-only panel or an ad-hoc structure only when a `system`
table genuinely can't express the state — and even then prefer *table + a panel
that renders it*, so SQL and the GUI never diverge.

**Composition, not contradiction.** This sits alongside "everything is replicated
state" (DR-1 / ARC-1): durable agreement still lives in the CRDT store and the
`system` table is its read view; **ephemeral / observed** state (a live cloud
inspect, the device registry) is a read view with no CRDT backing.

**Permission gate.** Cloud-derived `system` tables stay permission-gated
(deny-by-default, ask every time — see RULE-2 / PERM-2 and the CLAUDE.md cloud
hard rule): reading one must not trigger a real config-file read or cloud API call
without explicit, per-action consent.

See DR-1, ARC-1, TBL-7 (node_registry), ARC-12 (DDF exposed through the query
layer), RULE-2, PERM-2, ENT-32/ARC-13 (Provisioner). Engineering home:
`CLAUDE.md` → Conventions → "System tables — surface observable state as
`system.zetta_*` by default", and `docs/query.md`.
summary: Any state surfaced for inspection/observability (cluster nodes, deployments, models, jobs, cloud/provider state) defaults to a virtual, read-only system.zetta_* table computed at query time — not a bespoke GUI-only panel or a hand-synced copy.
title: Observable state defaults to a system.zetta_* table

**The first use case — a generic AI-project type.** Any team instantiates a churn project on *its own* data (define the entity, the churn label + horizon, the as-of date, the features). The pipeline is deliberately **simple, generic, and timeless**:

**featurize (point-in-time) → train (XGBoost) → explain (SHAP) → rank at-risk entities + per-entity drivers.**

Plus **optional, user-managed components** the project can include or omit:
- a **recommended-action** layer (driver → action + owner), and
- an **LLM playbook** narrator (constrained — writes the narrative + picks the play, never invents numbers).

**Generic, not bespoke:** the same project type serves any org's churn data; **Motive/Charles (PER-1) is the first instance**, not a special build. Even a basic model is useful — keep it simple. **The bar:** point at data → a working, explained churn model within ~an hour, deployed + governed.

Exercises the AI-project lifecycle: ingest (FEAT-1) → featurize + train (FEAT-6, learns from your data) → validate (FEAT-3, correctness) → deploy (FEAT-4) → run + monitor (FEAT-5) → governed self-serve (FEAT-9), under key-scoped access (RULE-3). The deeper agentic-RL extension is **deferred**. Built via a wtm worktree plan over its issues.

body:
The replication strategy chosen for a table or database.

**Variants**
- `ReplicateToAll` — every node holds a full copy (default; current behavior).
- `Partitioned` — rows are sharded across nodes by a `Partitioner`; each node holds a subset.
- `PartitionedWithReplicas(replication_factor)` — partitioned, with each partition replicated to `rf` nodes for fault tolerance.

The partition placement catalog ([[system.dataset_partitions]]) is always ReplicateToAll so placement is globally visible. Set via DDL (`CREATE TABLE ... WITH (replication=...)`) which lowers to an IR attribute. Extends the existing `ReplicationPolicy` seam.
summary: Per-table/database policy: ReplicateToAll | Partitioned | PartitionedWithReplicas(replication_factor).
title: ReplicationStrategy

body:
A unit of a partitioned table.

**Fields**
- `id` — partition id
- `table` — owning table
- `blob_ref` — the large-object id holding the partition's bytes (parquet/columnar) in the blob store
- `row_range` — rows covered
- `stats` — per-column stats (min/max/null counts) for pruning
- `owner_nodes` — node(s) currently holding this partition (per the replication strategy)

Produced by a [[Partitioner]] at load; tracked in [[system.dataset_partitions]] (ReplicateToAll). Compute runs on the node that owns the partition (compute-near-data).
summary: A shard of a partitioned table: id, table, large-object (blob) ref, row range, column stats, owning node(s).
title: Partition

body:
The seam that decides data placement.

**Responsibilities**
1. record → partition (hash of a key, or round-robin/surrogate for even balance)
2. partition → node(s) (rendezvous/consistent hashing so membership changes move ~1/N of partitions)

**Implementations (initial):** HashPartitioner, RoundRobinPartitioner (record→partition) + RendezvousPlacement (partition→node). **Future:** model-as-partitioner (a learned model performs the assignment). Fixed partition count P >> nodes so rebalance moves whole [[Partition]]s, not rehashes.
summary: Assigns a record to a partition and partitions to nodes; pluggable (hash/round-robin/rendezvous; model-driven later).
title: Partitioner

body:
A frontend that parses source text into the ExecutionGraph IR ([[ExecutionGraph]] / ENT-3).

**Implementations:** SQL dialect (exists); simulated-Python (ideal — calls/assignments/attribute-method chaining; **simulated libraries** such as a HuggingFace `datasets` shim emit IR ingest steps); optionally Lua/Orly (ADR-13).

No frontend is privileged — all lower to the same IR, which is gated and executed distributedly. The 'core API' is the IR + its executor.
summary: A parser that lowers source text (SQL / simulated-Python / Lua) into the ExecutionGraph IR; simulated libraries are frontend shims.
title: LanguageFrontend

body:
**Risk:** the native parquet reader (no Arrow) may not cover all encodings/compressions/edge cases in arbitrary parquet files, risking correctness or load failures, with ongoing maintenance as the format surface grows.

**Mitigation:** scope v1 to the encodings the target datasets use (plain/dictionary/RLE, snappy/zstd); golden parity tests vs Python (dev-time); fuzz/round-trip tests; clear errors on unsupported features; revisit vendoring Arrow only if coverage demands. Mirrors RSK-8 (native reimplementation correctness).

body: The extensibility model runs arbitrary code on nodes holding customer data. **Threat:** sandbox escape, capability over-grant, or egress would breach the 'no data leaves' promise. **Mitigation:** ADR-12 — capability-scoped deny-by-default sandbox, no fs/network egress by default, full audit, and approval gates for shared/enterprise-published extensions. body: Re-implementing training/inference/DDF algorithms natively can subtly diverge from reference implementations (numerical correctness, edge cases) and carries a maintenance burden as algorithms evolve. **Mitigation:** the correctness gate (ADR-3) and a verification suite (TP-1) comparing native outputs to reference results on known cases; scope native reimplementation to the algorithms that matter; treat Claude-Code-assisted ports as code that still must pass verification.
summary: Re-implementing ML/DDF algorithms in C++/CUDA risks numerical divergence from reference implementations and ongoing maintenance load.

body: Bursting many nodes raises three concerns: (1) **bulk identity** — minting + revoking N distinct short-lived node identities/capability tokens efficiently and without sprawl (open question on ADR-20/ADR-18); (2) **Spot/low-priority eviction** mid-training — jobs must tolerate node loss (checkpoint/restart); (3) **orphaned nodes** — a crashed orchestrator could leave paid nodes running. **Mitigation:** batch enrollment with TTL'd identities revoked on teardown; eviction-tolerant cluster-parallel jobs; a reconcile/reaper that reclaims nodes with no live owner; cost caps per burst.
summary: Provisioning 20+ ephemeral nodes at once strains identity issuance/revocation, exposes Spot-eviction failures mid-job, and risks orphaned nodes running up cost.
title: Ephemeral burst at scale: bulk identity, Spot eviction, orphaned-node cost

body:
**Given** a partitioned table over K partitions on M nodes,
**when** a node joins (or leaves),
**then** the Partitioner reassigns only ~1/N of partitions (rendezvous), blobs move to new owners, the system.dataset_partitions catalog reflects the new placement on every node, and every row remains readable exactly once (or rf times with replicas).
summary: A partitioned table places rows per the Partitioner; on node join/leave, partitions rebalance with minimal movement and no data loss.
title: Partition placement + rebalance-on-node-join correctness

body:
**Given** a partitioned table distributed across nodes,
**when** a DDF op (e.g. group-by / featurize / GBDT round) runs,
**then** each node computes over the partitions it owns locally and only partials/collectives cross the wire — verified by instrumenting bytes moved (≈ partials, not ≈ dataset) and by correctness vs a single-node oracle.
summary: A distributed DDF op executes against each node's locally-owned partitions and does not stream the whole dataset to one node.
title: Compute-near-data: an op runs on the node's local partition (no full-data pull)

body:
**Given** the `saas-sales-conversations` parquet (~100k×~3072 + binary `outcome`) and an Azure burst config with a cost cap,
**when** it is loaded as a partitioned table and the UC-1 engine (featurize→GBDT→TreeSHAP→rank) runs predicting `outcome`,
**then** the pipeline passes the correctness gate, runs compute-near-data across the (burst) cluster, produces a calibrated model + per-row drivers + ranked at-risk, and total burst cost ≤ cap. The capstone of UC-4 (burst-train on temporary nodes).
summary: End-to-end: load the HF dataset from parquet into a partitioned table, run UC-1 predicting outcome distributed across a burst Azure cluster, within the cost cap.
title: UC-1 at scale on saas-sales-conversations (parquet, partitioned, Azure burst, cost-capped)

body:
A REPL/notebook-style screen in the GUI control plane.

**Capabilities:** enter SQL or simulated-Python (incl. `datasets.load_dataset(...)`), execute against the cluster, view tabular results, errors, and history. Every statement lowers to the ExecutionGraph IR, passes the correctness gate, and is capability-scoped + audited (FEAT-9). Realizes the interactive side of UC-3 (ask an ad-hoc question, governed). Built from the [[REPL console (ImGui)]] component.
summary: Interactive console to run SQL or simulated-Python against the cluster; shows results/history; governed by capabilities + audit.
